adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:159-166 — eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees runs unguarded after prisma.booking.update already committed; a throw here leaves DB with new attendees but no calendar/video/email sync, no rollback (confidence=75, severity=P1).

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In addGuests.handler.ts, the code first persists new attendees via prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}}) and only afterward calls eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking) without a try/catch or a DB transaction. If updateCalendarAttendees throws, the mutation will error out while the DB changes (new attendees) are already committed, leaving the system in a partially-updated state (DB updated but calendar sync not performed; subsequent email sending is also skipped because it occurs after that call). Nothing in the diff indicates any rollback/transaction around these operations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:81-83 — partial-duplicate guest submissions are silently dropped with no feedback to the UI on which guests were skipped (confidence=90, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the server computes `uniqueGuests` by filtering out emails already in `booking.attendees` and any `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`. If at least one email remains, it proceeds to create attendees only for that filtered list and then returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` with no indication that some submitted emails were skipped. The UI always shows a generic success toast on mutation success, so a user can submit a mix of new + already-invited/blacklisted emails and receive no feedback about which ones were dropped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts — no check that booking isn't already cancelled/rejected/in the past before allowing guest additions (confidence=75, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `addGuestsHandler`, the booking is fetched by `id` and then updated (`prisma.booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`) and calendar/email side effects are triggered (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, `sendAddGuestsEmails`) without any guard on booking state (e.g., cancelled/rejected) or time (e.g., `startTime` already in the past). The handler has access to `booking.startTime/endTime` (scalar fields are selected by default) but does not check them, so the mutation will proceed even for bookings that are no longer actionable, which is a concrete correctness/behavior issue introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:169-172 — email send failures swallowed via console.log with no rethrow; mutation still reports success to the UI even if notification emails fail (confidence=75, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts`, the email notification step is wrapped in a `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` block and the error is neither rethrown nor returned to the client. Immediately after, the handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`, so the mutation will succeed from the UI’s perspective even if sending emails fails. This behavior (swallowing failures + reporting success) is directly observable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:46-48 — isTeamAdminOrOwner = isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...); since a user normally has exactly one team role, this branch is likely unsatisfiable, silently collapsing team-based authorization to only isOrganizer || isAttendee, wrongly denying legitimate team admins (confidence=75, severity=P1).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the variable is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but is computed with `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, meaning the user must satisfy both predicates to pass the team-based authorization path. In the subsequent permission gate (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) FORBIDDEN`), this effectively excludes users who are *only* team admins or *only* team owners from acting via team privileges. Unless `isTeamAdmin` is implemented to also return true for owners (not shown in the diff), this is a correctness/authorization bug introduced by the diff and contradicts the variable name/intent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:74-81,92-106 — dedup check reads booking.attendees snapshot then writes via createMany with no transaction/unique constraint tying read to write; concurrent addGuests calls can race and create duplicate attendee rows for the same email (TOCTOU) (confidence=75, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: The handler does a read (`findFirst` with `attendees`) then later writes (`booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`) and uses the initially-fetched `booking.attendees` to filter duplicates (`uniqueGuests`). That non-atomic pattern can indeed be subject to a TOCTOU race under concurrent calls. However, the proposed finding’s specific consequence (“can race and create duplicate attendee rows”) is not verifiable from this diff alone because it depends on whether the underlying DB schema enforces a unique constraint (e.g., `(bookingId,email)`) or whether Prisma `createMany` would error/skip duplicates. The diff does not show the attendee model or constraints, so the “duplicates will be created” claim is speculative.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:92-171 — three chained side effects (DB write, unguarded calendar sync, swallowed email errors) have inconsistent error-handling shapes, producing accidental rather than designed failure behavior (partial commits, silently dropped emails) (confidence=75, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the handler performs a DB update via prisma.booking.update (attendees createMany) and then immediately calls eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking) without any try/catch or transaction tying the DB write to the external calendar side effect. If calendar sync throws, the request fails after the DB has already been committed, leaving a partial/undesigned state (guests added in DB but not synced). Then email sending is wrapped in a try/catch that only console.logs and does not propagate or report the failure, so emails can be silently dropped while still returning success. This matches the finding’s claim of inconsistent error-handling across chained side effects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:108-120 — getTranslation called once per attendee inside a map over ALL attendees (not just new guests) on every add-guest call, an N+1-style pattern scaling with total attendee count (confidence=50, severity=P3).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts, attendeesListPromises is built via `bookingAttendees.attendees.map(async (attendee) => ({ ... language: { translate: await getTranslation(attendee.locale ?? "en", "common"), ... } }))`. This invokes `getTranslation` once per attendee, and `bookingAttendees.attendees` is the full attendee list after the update (existing + newly added). So on each add-guests call, the work scales with total attendee count and repeats translation loading for potentially identical locales, which is a verifiable inefficiency/N+1-style pattern in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:173 — returns hardcoded untranslated English string { message: "Guests added" } as part of API contract, inconsistent with i18n-key error pattern used elsewhere in the same handler (confidence=50, severity=P3).

adjudication.rationale: The handler does return a hardcoded English string (`return { message: "Guests added" };`). However, in the diff there is no evidence that this `message` field is part of a stable API contract or that any client consumes it (the new UI shows a toast using `t("guests_added")` in `AddGuestsDialog` and does not use the mutation response). The i18n-key pattern shown in the handler applies to TRPCError `message` values, not necessarily to success payloads. Therefore this is at most a consistency/style concern, not a clearly verifiable defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:36-41 — isTeamAdminOrOwner combining admin AND owner with logical AND is a new, narrower bespoke authorization rule invented for this feature, not reused from existing helpers, effectively authorization-model drift bundled into a feature PR (confidence=75, severity=P1).

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. This requires the user to be BOTH a team admin and a team owner to pass that branch, which is much narrower than the variable name suggests and is likely incorrect authorization logic (typically admin OR owner). As written, legitimate team admins (non-owners) would be denied, and the PR introduces a new bespoke combination rule for this endpoint rather than a shared “admin-or-owner” check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.schema.ts:4-5 — guests array has no max-length bound; combined with createMany + per-attendee sendEmail with no rate limit, any authenticated user can weaponize a booking as a spam/mail-relay vector by submitting thousands of emails (confidence=75, severity=P2).

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new authed TRPC mutation `viewer.bookings.addGuests` with input schema `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` that has no upper bound. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the server performs `attendees.createMany` with the provided emails (filtered only for already-attending and blacklist, but not capped), and then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` constructs `emailsToSend` including organizer/team notifications and then maps over `calendarEvent.attendees` to send an email per attendee via `sendEmail(...)`, with no rate limiting or batching shown. Therefore a permitted caller (organizer/attendee/team admin/owner) can submit a very large guests array to trigger mass DB inserts and mass outbound email sends, making a spam/mail-relay style abuse vector. The finding is grounded in the diff; the only overstatement is "any authenticated user" (access is constrained to related users), but the underlying unbounded-email abuse risk is real.

addGuests.handler.ts:73-77 — eventManager uses the requesting user's calendar credentials (not organizer's) to update the calendar event, reachable by non-organizer attendees; trust-boundary inconsistency (confidence=50, severity=P3).

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the mutation explicitly allows non-organizer callers (an attendee: `const isAttendee = ...; if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;`). Later, it builds the calendar updater using the requesting user: `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user); const eventManager = new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] }); await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);`. Since `booking.userId` (organizer) can differ from `ctx.user.id` (attendee), this means a non-organizer attendee can trigger calendar-updating logic that runs under their own connected calendar credentials rather than the organizer’s, which is a verifiable trust-boundary/correctness issue introduced by the diff (at minimum: organizer calendar may not be updated unless organizer calls; behavior depends on caller).

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:74-78 — dedup filter doesn't normalize case (Guest@x.com vs guest@x.com), risking near-duplicate attendee rows (confidence=50, severity=P3).

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In addGuests.handler.ts the `uniqueGuests` filter compares `guest === attendee.email` without normalizing case, so `Guest@x.com` and `guest@x.com` will be treated as different and can both be inserted via `createMany`. Nothing else in the diff lowercases/normalizes `guests` before this check (zod only validates format). This also affects the blacklist check since the blacklist is lowercased but `guest` is not, so case-variant blacklisted emails may slip through.
